prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks into persistent credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed from B036 (Melitz and Helpman) to B040 (Kiyotaki and Moore). The reason is the weighing of criteria in this exchange, not the support counts. In round 1 I ranked B040 second and said I would not oppose it if the committee put clean attribution above empirical grounding. The chair's questions ask which criterion each member ranks first, and mine is maturity combined with a defensible credit boundary. On that test B040 is stronger. Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) isolate one general mechanism: borrowing limits tied to collateral value feed back on asset prices, so small shocks become persistent and large. It has had close to three decades of extension, criticism and use in macro-finance, crisis analysis and policy models. Its originating paper has two authors, and every B040 proposal in the files names the same pair, so a two-person part matches the credit without an arbitrary cut. B036 has two decades of testing, but its central weakness is that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, the co-originators of the firm-level trade evidence that the model rationalised, fall outside any three-name cap. Boppart and I both concede this. I cannot resolve it by argument, and a prize that rests on that cut would invite avoidable dispute. On the 2022 overlap, I read the earlier prize as concerning banks, bank runs and the empirical study of financial crises. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values and asset prices create a real-economy feedback loop. That is a different mechanism, although the committee has not verified the comparison in this stage and I rely on general knowledge. I would draft the citation around the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles and crises are modelled, not around the quantitative size of amplification, which is not settled.
statement.case_against: The empirical record is the strongest reservation. As someone who weights new measurement and evidence, I am uneasy that direct validation of collateral-constraint amplification is more indirect than the theory's influence suggests, and the quantitative importance of the mechanism in macro models is still contested. The award would honour a conceptual mechanism and leave out the more empirical financial-accelerator strand of Gertler and Gilchrist, which Dreber-Almenberg rightly says the committee should state openly. The 2022 prize may also be thought to cover financial frictions closely enough to lower the marginal case, and the contribution rests heavily on one seminal paper and its extensions. B036 and B044 are both credible rivals. B036 introduced a testable reallocation channel that is distinct from the 2008 trade recognition. B044 offers directly identified evidence with a decade of replication, and its trade-shock core of Autor, Dorn and Hanson is now agreed among its supporters. Both are weaker than B040 on attribution or maturity in my judgement, but not by a wide margin.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B040 with Kiyotaki and Moore, qualifies his opening wording so that excluding Gertler and Gilchrist rests on the independent origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism and not on prior recognition of the accelerator, and in round 1 doubted that B036 is distinct from Krugman's trade prize.
responses.response: I accept his qualification and it matches how I now frame B040. The case for a two-name part is the clean origin of the mechanism, and the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist should not be defended by saying the accelerator was already recognised. On B036 I still think the Melitz-Helpman mechanism is distinct from increasing-returns trade theory, but that was never my main problem with it. The unresolved credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is what moved me to B040 once the committee had to choose a single part.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B036 with Helpman and Melitz, keeps B040 as his main alternative, concedes that the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is the strongest reservation, and argues that the explanatory model counts for more than the earlier descriptive exporter-premium evidence.
responses.response: I agree with his weighting of the model over the descriptive facts, and I made that argument myself in round 1. But on a three-name cap the weighting does not remove the attribution problem. It only explains why the model deserves credit. We both rank B040 as the alternative and both concede its cleaner claim, so I am acting on that concession. I also note, without making it a point for either side, that his round-1 uncertainty asks whether B040's cleaner attribution should outweigh B036 once the 2022 overlap is weighed. My answer is yes, because I read the 2022 overlap as narrower than he does.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg supports B040, calls the empirical validation gap the most serious reservation against it, and wants the citation drafted around the mechanism and its influence on how crises are modelled, with the Committee stating openly that excluding Gertler and Gilchrist favours theory over tested evidence.
responses.response: I agree and adopt both points. My citation names the mechanism and not any measured magnitude, and I would want the committee record to say that the part recognises a theoretical mechanism and its influence. The cost of leaving out the empirical accelerator strand is real. I accept it for the sake of attribution, and I do not think adding Gertler or Gilchrist would improve the claim, because it would widen the overlap with earlier financial-crisis recognition and blur the origin of the idea.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B044 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson, anchors the citation on empirical evidence about trade and technology exposure, and argues that a decade of replication and refinement answers the recency objection.
responses.response: His case is strong and I moved toward B044 in my own thinking. The trio is now a clean attribution for the China-shock papers, the identification is transparent, and I agree that refinement without reversal is the right test. I still weigh B040 above it, for two reasons. The shift-share inference debate and the dispute over size, persistence and the trade-versus-automation split are still active. His own uncertainty list also leaves open whether the task framework and the trade-shock evidence are one achievement or two. A decade is a respectable record, but it is shorter than three decades. I list B044 as an alternative and would not oppose it if the committee judged direct identification to outweigh conceptual generality.

uncertainties: Whether the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the marginal case for Kiyotaki and Moore more than I judge. My view that the mechanisms are distinct rests on general knowledge, and the committee has not verified it.
How much weight indirect and mixed empirical validation of collateral-constraint amplification should carry against conceptual generality and demonstrated influence.
Whether leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist undervalues the more empirical financial-accelerator strand.
Whether the committee will accept the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum if B036 is revisited, and whether Helpman or Redding is the better second name.
Whether the task framework and the China-shock evidence in B044 form one achievement or two, and how persistent and large the trade-shock effects are under shift-share inference.
My assessment relies on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 files, not independent verification of citations, replication or impact.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for Kiyotaki, Moore or the other credited names. My supplied profile lists no co-authorship or institutional tie to them, and my research is in economic history, so B040 lies outside my field. My earlier first choice, B036, also had no profile tie. I disclose that my Lund colleague Tommy Andersson prefers B040. That is an institutional connection with a committee member and not a tie to any candidate, and I formed this change of view from the arguments in the files. This is a self-reported disclosure and is not adjudicated.
